title: How to Turn a Side Hustle into an Investment Fund (U.S. Plan)
description: Leveraging the Solo 401(k) to save 100% of your side income tax-deferred.
content:
For many US employees, a 'side hustle' (consulting, Uber, Etsy) is just extra spending money. But for the financially savvy, it is a tax shelter. Because side hustle income is considered 'Self-Employment Income', it opens the door to business retirement accounts like the **Solo 401(k)**. This vehicle allows you to contribute massive amounts—far more than a standard employee 401(k)—essentially letting you live on your day job salary while funneling your entire side hustle income into tax-advantaged investments.

Key Takeaways

  • The Double Contribution: As both employee and employer of your side hustle, you can contribute up to $69,000 (2025 limit) or 100% of your net earnings, whichever is less.
  • Tax Arbitrage: You can use side hustle expenses (home office, laptop) to lower taxable income, then put the rest in a pre-tax 401(k) to lower it further.
  • Roth Option: Solo 401(k)s often allow Roth contributions (Mega Backdoor), unlike SEP IRAs.
  • Asset Protection: 401(k)s have stronger legal protection against creditors/lawsuits than IRAs.

Why It Matters (US Context)

If you have a W-2 job with a 401(k) and a Side Hustle with a Solo 401(k), the 'Employee' limit ($23,500) is shared between them. However, the 'Employer' profit sharing limit is separate. This means you can max out your W-2 match AND put 20% of your side hustle profits into the Solo 401(k).

The Solo 401(k) Mechanics

This is the most powerful account for solopreneurs.

Eligibility

You must have self-employment activity (EIN not strictly required, but recommended) and NO common-law employees (except a spouse). If you hire a full-time assistant, you lose Solo 401(k) eligibility.

Contribution Math

Example: You make $80k at a Day Job and $30k Consulting.

  • Day Job: You contribute $23,500 to W-2 401(k). You hit the 'Employee' cap.
  • Side Hustle: You can contribute 0% as 'Employee' (cap hit). BUT, you can contribute ~20% of net profit as 'Employer'.
  • Result: You shelter ~$6,000 of side income from taxes entirely.

Scenario B: The Side Hustle makes $100k. You can put away $23.5k (Employee) + $20k (Employer) = $43.5k total. Nearly half your income vanishes from the IRS's view.

How to execute the '100% Invested' Plan

  1. Open a Business Checking Account: Keep side money separate. It makes tax time easier.
  2. Open Solo 401(k): Go to Fidelity, Schwab, or E-Trade. You will need an EIN (get it free from IRS.gov). Note: Vanguard's Solo 401(k) does not allow IRA rollovers or loans, so it is less flexible.
  3. Pay Business Expenses First: Software, mileage, internet portion. This lowers Net Income.
  4. Sweep the Rest: Calculate Net Profit. Transfer the maximum allowable amount to the Solo 401(k) before tax day. Invest it in VTSAX/VTI.
  5. Live on W-2: Do not upgrade your lifestyle with side money. Treat the side hustle as a 'Wealth Venture Capital Firm', not a piggy bank.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a deadline to open?

Yes. You must open the Solo 401(k) by December 31st to contribute for that tax year. You can fund it up until Tax Day (April 15), but the account must exist by Dec 31.

What if I need the money?

Solo 401(k)s allow you to take a loan of up to $50,000 (or 50% of balance) from yourself. You pay the interest back to yourself. It is a great liquidity backup.

Is SEP IRA easier?

Yes, less paperwork. But SEP IRAs don't allow 'Employee' contributions (only Employer 25%). If your side hustle makes $20k, a Solo 401(k) lets you save nearly 100% of it (if under the global cap). A SEP only lets you save 25% ($5k). Solo 401(k) wins for small side hustles.
